h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to judge which settings are strong, weak or neutral, and which parts other settings can cut off from the outcome. Build hypotheses mainly from (a) the edited field's current parent value: replacing a strong value with a weak one hurts, and filling an empty or harmful slot helps; and (b) conditions that disconnect the edited part, pushing its effect toward zero. Directions refer to the signed effect, not its size. Disconnection makes the effect lower only if the edit usually helps, and higher if it usually hurts. If the usual sign is unclear, do not use it. When finding flaws, check this sign logic first. Replace any hypothesis whose direction could reverse through a competing effect or that relies on partial redundancy. Vary edit fields and values. State a one-sentence mechanism.

hyps.why: Filling an empty direct input-output edge with a strong conv adds a new path, a bigger gain than replacing an existing op.
Filling an empty edge into the output with a strong conv restores a path and gives a larger gain.
Activating a dead edge with a strong conv helps more than swapping one op for another.
Edge 0 gates two downstream paths, so filling it with a conv adds substantial capacity.
Removing a strong conv on the direct edge hurts more than removing a weak op or a no-op.
Deleting a strong conv into the output hurts much more than deleting a weak op.
Removing a strong conv on the input edge cripples two paths, worse than removing a weak op.
With edge 0 removed, node 1 carries no signal so edge 2 is disconnected and its usually beneficial edit does nothing.
Edge 4 has no input when edge 0 is none, so a conv there cannot add its usual gain.
Filling an empty edge into the output with a conv restores a path and beats the gain from replacing an existing op.
